content: An infinitive is a verb with no subject and
no person — the plain 'to X' form. English
needs two words for it, Latin an ending.
This card's own sentence hangs three of
them off a single main verb:
agere ... explēre ... mūnīre
= to bring up ... to fill ... to build
You have been reading them since Tier 1,
wherever possum or volō needed a second
verb:
Hoc facere possum. = I can do this.
What arrives now is the rest of the
family. That plain -re form is one of six.
The present active infinitive is the second
part printed in every verb card's cue:
-āre   amāre    to love
-ēre   vidēre   to see
-ere   regere   to rule
-īre   audīre   to hear
Shift that ending to -rī — or, in the
short -ere class, to a bare -ī — and the
sense turns passive:
amārī   to be loved
regī    to be ruled
audīrī  to be heard
A few everyday verbs keep older shapes:
esse (be), posse (be able), velle (want),
ferre (bear), īre (go).
Two more tenses, each with its own shape.
PERFECT active — -isse:
vīdisse      to have seen
tulisse      to have carried
PERFECT passive — participle + esse:
captus esse  to have been captured
FUTURE active — -ūrus + esse:
ventūrus esse  to be about to come
The tense is measured against the main
verb, not against you: vidēre is going on
or general, vīdisse is over and done.
Recognition only: naming which member of
the family a shape belongs to.
English reports speech with 'that' and a
full clause: 'Statius writes that he
wants to live with his father.'
Latin has no 'that' here. The reported
subject goes into the ACCUSATIVE and its
verb into the INFINITIVE. This card's own
sentence, word for word:
Scrībit Statius illum cum patre
habitāre velle.
= Statius writes that he wants to
live with his father.
illum is the accusative subject; velle is
the infinitive, with habitāre hanging off
velle in turn. Nothing else fences the
reported clause off — those two shapes
are the whole signal.
The verbs that open a reported clause are
already in hand: dīcō (say), putō
(think), sciō (know), crēdō (believe),
audiō (hear), spērō (hope).
The infinitive's tense is measured against
that verb: present = same time, perfect =
earlier, future = later.
Lēgātus dīcit mīlitēs gladiōs acuere.
= The officer says the soldiers are
sharpening their swords.
Dīcunt eum aurum domum tulisse.
= They say he carried the gold home.
Nēmō crēdit hanc pācem diūturnam
futūram esse.
= No one believes this peace will be
lasting.
Reading one is a two-step habit:
1. find the accusative
2. find the infinitive
Then read that pair as the subject and verb
of a clause sitting inside the sentence.
The accusative there is not the object of
the main verb. Dīcunt eum vēnisse does
not say they said him; it says they say
he came.
esse is often dropped and understood:
Putō eum fortem. = I think he is brave.
Recognition only: reading a reported
clause, never building one.
